title: Sterling Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Sterling wells have a 70-foot median depth, 15 gpm median yield, and typical finished costs of $8,400-$15,800.
h1: What Sterling, Colorado Wells Usually Cost and Produce
intro_html:
Buying land or a house near Sterling means looking closely at the well record, not just the listing description. Within 5 miles of Sterling, Colorado, DWR records show 3,110 permitted wells. Of those, 2,198 report a total depth, 480 report a pump yield, and 103 report a static water level.

The local pattern is relatively favorable for water production: the median reported well yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, and 91% of reported yields are above 15 gallons per minute. Depth is less uniform than that yield figure suggests, so a nearby well is useful evidence but not a guarantee for a new hole.

sections.heading: Sterling wells are usually shallow, but the range is wide
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Sterling is 70 feet. The middle half runs from 45 to 90 feet, and 80% of wells are under 100 feet. That is the profile a driller will usually start with when estimating a straightforward site in the plains and alluvial setting around Sterling.

There are exceptions. The 90th-percentile depth is 144 feet, while the deepest record reaches 3,230 feet. The aquifer names on permits are mostly unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 2,800 wells, while 149 are listed as alluvial and 38 as Ogallala. A bid should account for the actual parcel, nearby logs, casing and grout requirements, and the possibility that local conditions differ from the median.

sections.heading: Reported Sterling yields are strong, but confirm the test
sections.html:
Among the 480 Sterling-area records that report a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is also 15.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute, and 91% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Nine percent fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. No records in this dataset report less than 5 gallons per minute.

Those figures describe reported well tests, not a promise for an unbuilt well. Ask for the original test, test duration, static and pumping levels, and the permitted use. A household well also needs suitable storage, pressure equipment, and a pump sized to the well rather than simply to the reported yield. Domestic and household permits make up 58% of the local use mix.

sections.heading: Sterling water levels show variation, not a simple decline
sections.html:
The median static water level is 21 feet below ground surface, with the middle half from 8 to 37 feet. That is useful for planning pump setting, trenching, and well construction, but static water level is a measurement from a particular well and date. It can vary across a property and with seasonal conditions.

The decade series does not show a clean, continuous downward trend. Median depth to water was 16 feet in the 1950s, 13 feet in the 1960s, 42 feet in the 1970s, 29 feet in the 2010s, and 28 feet in the 2020s. The limited number of records with water-level data means a buyer should compare nearby well logs and obtain a current measurement rather than treating the series as a site-specific forecast.

sections.heading: Sterling has a long permit and drilling history
sections.html:
Permits were issued across every decade from the 1950s through the 2020s, and the newest permit year in the records is 2025. The largest decade totals were 450 permits in the 2000s, 424 in the 1990s, and 356 in the 1970s. That history gives a buyer more local records to review than a newly developing area would typically provide.

The most active named driller in these records is Stewart Drilling Co., also listed as Stewart, Dennis W., with 527 records. Authorized (Pe, Pg) appears on 319, and Canfield, Leslie George appears on 240. These names describe permit records, not a recommendation. Verify the current license, scope of work, insurance, and references before hiring anyone.

sections.heading: A Sterling well may cost $8,400 to $15,800 finished
sections.html:
For Sterling's alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 70-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $2,400 to $3,800. That is only the hole. A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $8,400 to $15,800.

Use the local depth distribution when comparing bids. A proposal based on 70 feet may be reasonable for many sites, while a parcel requiring more than 100 feet can move beyond the median estimate. Ask what happens if the driller must continue, whether casing and grout are included, and which electrical or trenching conditions are excluded. Permit, water-rights, septic, and site-development work should be priced separately unless the contract says otherwise.

sections.heading: Check contamination, septic layout, and dry-hole exposure
sections.html:
Within about 10 miles of Sterling, the mapped environmental information includes 19 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 6 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not establish that a particular well is contaminated, but it is a reason to review the parcel's environmental history and test the water before closing. Do not rely only on a general statement that the water is safe.

Low-yield records are absent from this dataset, but that does not eliminate dry-hole risk on a new site. Confirm the driller's dry-hole terms and the intended well location. Septic setbacks, replacement-area needs, driveway access, power routing, and building placement can all affect the total project. A Colorado DWR permit and an exempt household-use well are not the same as a guarantee of water quality or construction success.

sections.heading: Before buying or building near Sterling, verify the parcel
sections.html:
Start with the exact legal location and pull neighboring DWR permits, construction reports, yield tests, and water-level measurements. Compare wells near the property with the broader Sterling pattern: a 70-foot median depth, 45-to-90-foot middle half, and 15.0-gallon-per-minute median reported yield. The nearby records are evidence for planning, not a guarantee that geology will match from one lot to the next.

For a new build, have the well location, septic area, driveway, utility trench, and house footprint reviewed together. Confirm the permitted use, anticipated household demand, pump and storage design, and water-testing plan. In an over-appropriated basin, determine whether an augmentation plan or other water-rights requirement applies before construction. That review is especially important for irrigation or expanded use, since local permits include domestic, stock, irrigation, and monitoring uses.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Sterling, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Sterling is 70 feet. The middle half of reported depths is 45 to 90 feet, and 80% are under 100 feet. Some wells are much deeper, with the deepest record reaching 3,230 feet, so nearby well logs should guide a site-specific estimate.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Sterling, Colorado?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 70-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $2,400 to $3,800. A finished well including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $8,400 to $15,800. Actual bids depend on depth, casing, access, and site conditions.

faq.q: How much water do Sterling wells produce?
faq.a: Of the 480 local records reporting a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 15.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute, and 91% report more than 15 gallons per minute. These are reported test results, not a guarantee for a new well, so request the original yield test.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Sterling?
faq.a: The well records do not prove that any individual well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, mapped information includes 19 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 6 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the specific well before closing and periodically after purchase, using a laboratory and a panel appropriate to the property's history.

faq.q: Do Sterling wells have enough water for a new home?
faq.a: Local records show a 15.0-gallon-per-minute median reported yield, with 91% of reported yields above 15 gallons per minute. That is encouraging for planning, but household suitability also depends on the permit, pump, storage, water quality, and intended use. Confirm the permitted use and any augmentation-plan requirements before adding irrigation or expanding demand.
